A massive improvement over Bleed 1, as well as one of the most satisfying 2D action titles I’ve had the pleasure of encountering. Bleed 2 really gets the basics right, offering snappy and stylish gameplay that makes you feel like a total boss whether you’re dodging tons of bullets with precise dashes in slo-mo, reflecting enemy attacks with kick-ass katana parries or melting a boss down in seconds using powerful, responsive weaponry.

At the same time, it’s a surprisingly in-depth game, having a huge amount of variation that allows to replay its 7 levels (plus some bonus modes) over and over again without getting stale. Each difficulty setting raises the bar noticeably and meaningfully, with not just speed and damage but almost every single boss pattern getting beefed up. Furthermore, you get 6 playable characters, and most of their movesets are unique enough to show the same set pieces in a completely different light.

The game also oozes with effortless, light-hearted charm thanks to its unobtrusive sense of humor, quality pixel art and simple yet well-presented story. There are basically only 4 characters with personalities here, but each of them is bound to leave you smiling at least once. Wryn is a chill, likeable, relatable gaming hero, Rival is perfect in his new role of a hesitant sidekick, Valentine works great as a smug villain who gets taken down a notch immediately, and Plucky is the very definition of adorable.

Whether you play it for 1 or 100 hours, this is a wonderful experience.

Sometimes, what you want is a deep and emotional indie game, with a gut wrenching story and an immersive atmosphere, so it can draw you in, expand your notions of what a video game can be, and make you reflect about life and the nature of reality. Other times, however, all you really want is some dumb, epic, high octane fun. If you're looking for the former, look elsewhere, but if you're looking for the latter, Bleed 2 fits the bill perfectly.

I originally got this game as part of an itch bundle a long time ago, and only opened its Steam page to see what people were saying about it. It made me kind of sad to see it only had about 400 reviews 'cause, without mincing words, Bleed 2 is F**KING AWESOME and deserves a lot more recognition. After seeing that small review count, I HAD to buy it again just so I could give it a review of my own.

Bleed 2 has the energy of all those ridiculously over-the-top action cartoons and anime from the 80s and 90s, and I'm here for it. Levels vary wildly between hopping on car roofs in a busy highway while shooting hoverbike baddies, having a duel against a freaking Ninja on top of an airplane, platforming on moving missiles while being shot at by a bazooka wielding weirdo, a zero-gravity duel against a menacing robot guardian, and a final duel involving rocket launchers, katanas and infinite-ammo pistols. The pacing stays up throughout the entire thing, and it is all accompanied by this AMAZING electro-speed-metal soundtrack that really keeps the blood pumping and me wanting more. I added the soundtrack to this game to my gym playlist on Spotify, best decision ever.

The player character is a girl called Wryn, who is like all the most badass action heroes from movies and cartoons had a baby. She wields infinite ammo pistols, a freaking katana that can deflect bullets, and this crazy pair of boots that allow her to effortlessly zip around in the air. Oh, did I mention she can also slow down the flow of time? Yeah! Anyway, one day, Wryn's just chilling in her home playing videogames, when duty abruptly calls her: shots are being fired, everyone is panicking, aliens are invading, things are exploding, and stuff is getting intense. That's when Wryn jumps right into action, starts killing all kinds of crazy foes, and only stops when she finishes the job. The story has this clearly tongue-in-cheek tone that makes the most of its absurd setting, making it hilarious, fun, and even a bit endearing at times.

Now, none of the above really matters if the game doesn't play well, right? Well, luckily, it does play well! The controls are fluid and responsive, the level design is fun and fast-paced, the bosses are challenging and varied, and the pacing never, never, NEVER slows down. Wryn is clearly the kind of girl that is only ever gonna stop when she's dead, and that ain't happening anytime soon. 

I played the entire thing on Very Hard in my very first playthrough, because it's well worth it. While the levels and bosses are definitely challenging, the game is really generous with checkpoints, so you can keep trying stuff until you win, making it way more worthwhile to play on the hardest setting right from the get-go. I wish more hard games were like that, just letting you continue from the boss fight you lost, instead of forcing you to go through the entire stage again.

If I were to make a complaint, it's that the game is really short. Sure, there's some extra characters to unlock, some varied weapons to try out, and even a freaking roguelike mode, which do add some replay value, but at the end of the day, I just wish the game had more story levels.

All in all, though, definitely a badass masterpiece. Get this if you want some AWESOME action platforming to keep you company in these cold/hot (depending on your hemisphere) months.

tl;dr: VERY short game. Fun semi-retro arcade-y action. 2-player co-op available. Reasonable price.

Something to bear in mind that may turn some people away: this game is very short. I played through the story mode 4 times within 3.1 hours. I'm reminded of 16 bit smhups and beat-em-ups, though Bleed 2 is much more forgiving. Story mode has infinite lives and frequent checkpoints, so dying isn't too frustrating.

The game is all about peppering enemies with bullets, reflecting enemy bullets, slowing time, air-dashing, and some simple platforming. The main focus is the boss battles; it reminds me a lot of classic Treasure games like Gunstar Heroes. There's unlockable characters and weapons for some replay value, and 2-player co-op (though I never tried it).

The difficulty settings are actually very well done, imo. It's not just more/less hp/damage, there are a number of subtle (and not so subtle) changes with each setting. Higher difficulties = faster bullets, more hp for enemies, additional boss patterns, and more alternate-colored bullets (relevant for most but not all characters). I liked these differences and it made my playthroughs different enough to not bore me to death. 

There are 5 additional characters to unlock, though 1 is a recolor of the default (which does affect gamelpay somewhat), and 2 of them can change out their weapons and dash abilities (I didn't use weapons besides the default though). The characters are decently distinct from each other. 1 of them turns the game into Ikaruga, 1 of them is pure melee with hp regen abilities, and so on.

I only played the story mode, so I can't speak to the other modes. In theory, they add replay value, but yeah I can't say.

All told, Bleed 2 is a good time. A short time, very short, but a good time. Whether 10 buck is worth that is up to you of course. If it's on sale and you'd like a slice of arcade-y action, pick it up!

I followed Bleed 2 on BootDiskRevolution's own website, noting the GIF's and text he shared about troubleshooting and considering the game mechanics, where fun falls between doable and challenging, his interesting solutions, and so on.

When Bleed 2 finally released I had to play it... after I got an income wherein $10 actually was affordable for me.

Let me say that the thoughtfulness and tweaking glimpsed in those online journals has paid off. Bleed 2 is very workings-based, with hitboxes and timing worth knowing. It even has an option in the menu for playing to learn the hitboxes, "Under the Hood".

There's much else I could gush about: the multiple playable dimoch's who actually are interesting and unique to play, an improvement over the alternatives in Bleed 1; the simulator levels that mix it up and test skill; and the greatly improved environmental imagery and animations, as well as Wryn's own animations; and  yet I'd like to avoid spoiling anything.

I at least warn for anyone who played Bleed 1 that Bleed 2 is immensely faster-paced. Its also more focused; the swaths of weapons from 1, most redundant and underwhelming, have been traded off for just a few to choose from, and you can clear the entire game without choosing any of the few, quality-focused alternatives presented.

The function of doing one deflecting slash before opening fire is very well-implemented in my opinion, and it works well for making defense and retaliation a rewarding experience.

---

The main other pros to list are small things. Namely, nods by Ian Campbell to his own past work. For those of us who've looked into his stuff and actually been charmed, it's actually warming to see him wear his own history as a coding hobby-man on his sleeve. Dimoch's from his past games can be found in here, including enemies from the first Bleed who actually seem to remember what happened last time, and including one other who essentially tells most of the story.

Wordless storytelling in the levels themselves is impressive in my opinion. Although not as impactful or impression-leaving as Sonic 3& Knuckles in my opinion, impressive things do still happen and are pulled off engagingly.

----

The "cons" I have in mind come down only to my taste; others probably consider them positives.

First, the first Bleed, had speech bubbles and scenes that let us meet Wryn and learn more about her 
 quirky and charmingly evil nature. No such thing here. Wryn barely even talks until the last chapter, and there's no development or change. I guess in this game she's really mostly just doing her job and defending her title. Even the after-KO speech bubbles seem to be less diverse and less about her own personality leaking through, though it does compensate by Wryn occasionally seeming aware of what, specifically, just did her in. 

For those of charmed by her who wanted to read more from her, this is a bit of a letdown to say the least.

Secondly, while the environmental art and in-game animation of all things, Wryn included, is improved, Wryn's actual drawn self in the like of scenes, promo material, and the menu animation, looks worse than in 1. It's almost as if Mr. Campbell did everything else first, realized he had no up-close Wryn art, just yelled "screw it", and slopped out what he could on belief that nobody would care.

With Wryn herself being highly abbreviated already, and there almost being no non-gameplay pics of her, it's understandable. However, like with the original Powerpuff Girls, even if she looks cartoonish, her original proportions still matter, and if that's dismissed it's possible to be drawn in a way that looks awkward. No deal breaker by any means, but a bit of a letdown.

___

All the same, I strongly recommend Bleed 2 to any high-skill-kind gamers. I also recommend it to any fans of Bleed 1 who want to see what's next for their beloved superpowered serial killer, although I doubt you'll feel impelled to lunge forward and hug her through the computer monitor like last time.

Not as much of a charming surprise as the first, but there's undeniably more to this one in almost every way. It's a little more all over the place as a result too, but it all comes down to whether or not you feel that 'the same again but more of it' is enough -- in this case, it was for me.
